title: Deriving hydrostatic pressure difference
prior_knowledge_summary: Pressure is normal force per unit area.
Density is mass per unit volume.
Weight is the force mg, and a static object or region has zero resultant force.
The previous lesson related force, pressure and area for a uniform pressure on a stated area.
new_learning: Derive hydrostatic pressure difference from the definitions of pressure and density.
Explain why the vertical depth difference, rather than the container area or the total liquid volume, determines the pressure difference in a static liquid of uniform density.
not_yet_taught: Extended calculations that solve for density or depth

visual_planning.reason: Six planned sketches each have a distinct teaching job: opening comparison, column inventory, cancellation chain, two-depth force balance, misconception comparison and synthesis.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: Wide tank or narrow tube?
content: Imagine a wide tank and a narrow tube filled with the same liquid to the same vertical depth. The wide tank contains much more liquid, so it is tempting to predict a larger pressure increase at its base.
The surprising result is that the pressure difference from surface to base is the same. We need to find where the extra liquid weight goes and why area disappears from the final result.

figure.brief: Place a narrow vertical tube and a wide tank side by side. Both contain the same liquid to equal labelled depth h. Show a question mark beside each base and no pressure values or conclusion.
figure.alt_text: A narrow tube and a wide tank contain the same liquid to equal depth.

blocks.title: Three ideas join the chain
content: Density is mass per unit volume. In ρ = m/V, ρ is density in kg m⁻³, m is mass in kg and V is volume in m³. Rearranging gives m = ρV.
Weight is a formula to remember: W = mg. W is weight in N and g is acceleration of free fall in N kg⁻¹ or m s⁻².
Pressure is normal force per unit area. In p = F/A, p is pressure in Pa, F is the normal force in N and A is area in m².
The derivation will move through volume, mass, weight and pressure in that order.

figure.purpose: Connect the controlled definitions to one liquid column
figure.brief: Draw a straight liquid column of area A and height h. Beside it, show a short arrow chain V = Ah, m = rho V, W = mg, p = F/A. Do not show the completed hydrostatic formula.
figure.alt_text: A liquid column links volume, mass, weight and pressure.

blocks.title: First derivation: surface to base
content: Take a vertical-sided column of static liquid with cross-sectional area A and depth h. Its volume is V = Ah.
Use density to find its mass: m = ρV = ρAh.
Its weight is W = mg = ρAhg. This weight produces the extra normal force on the base due to the liquid column.
Use pressure as force divided by area: p = F/A = ρAhg/A.
The area A cancels, leaving p = ρgh. For a surface-to-base comparison, this p is the pressure difference caused by the liquid. It is not an absolute pressure model.
Unit check: (kg m⁻³)(N kg⁻¹)(m) = N m⁻² = Pa. The dimensions match pressure.

figure.purpose: Make the cancellation in the derivation visible
figure.brief: Create an annotated calculation ladder for a liquid column: V = Ah, m = rho Ah, W = rho Ahg, p = rho Ahg/A. Cross out the matching A factors and finish with p = rho gh. Include units in a separate check line.
figure.alt_text: A derivation ladder shows the column area cancelling to give pressure proportional to depth.

blocks.title: Second derivation: between any two depths
content: Now choose two horizontal levels inside the same static liquid. Let the upper pressure be p₁ and the lower pressure be p₂. Imagine a vertical liquid slab of area A between them, with vertical separation Δh.
The lower liquid pushes upward on the slab with force p₂A. The upper liquid pushes downward with force p₁A. The slab's weight is ρAΔhg downward.
The slab is stationary, so upward force equals total downward force: p₂A = p₁A + ρAΔhg.
Cancel A and rearrange: p₂ - p₁ = ρgΔh.

Hydrostatic pressure difference is a formula to remember: Δp = ρgΔh. Here Δp is the pressure increase in Pa when moving downward by vertical depth difference Δh in m through a static liquid of uniform density ρ in kg m⁻³.

figure.purpose: Show the force balance that produces a pressure difference
figure.brief: Draw an imaginary rectangular liquid slab between two horizontal levels. Label upward lower-face force p2 A, downward upper-face force p1 A, downward weight rho A delta-h g and the separation delta-h. Show no absolute pressure values.
figure.alt_text: An imaginary liquid slab is balanced by pressure forces and its weight.

blocks.title: A numerical check of the derivation
content: Consider water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. Compare two points whose vertical depths differ by 0.30 m. Use g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.
Δp = ρgΔh = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.30 = 2943 Pa, or 2.9 × 10³ Pa to two significant figures.

If the imaginary slab area were 0.020 m², its weight would be ρAΔhg = 58.9 N. The difference between the two pressure forces would be ΔpA = 2943 × 0.020 = 58.9 N. This independent force check matches the slab's weight.
Both routes give the same result because pressure difference multiplied by area must balance the slab weight.

figure.purpose: Check the pressure result through an independent force balance
figure.brief: Use two aligned calculation panels. Panel one computes delta-p from rho g delta-h. Panel two multiplies delta-p by area and compares it with rho A delta-h g. Carry all units and highlight the matching 58.9 N values.
figure.alt_text: Pressure-difference and force-balance calculations give the same force.

blocks.title: Why more liquid does not automatically mean more pressure difference
content: The idea that a wider container must give a larger pressure difference feels reasonable because the wider liquid column weighs more.
It fails because that larger weight is spread over a proportionally larger base area. Doubling A doubles the weight ρAhg and also doubles the area in p = F/A, so the ratio is unchanged.

For a static liquid of uniform density, only the vertical separation between the two levels appears in Δp = ρgΔh. A longer sloping route or a larger total liquid volume does not increase Δp when the two vertical levels stay fixed.
This result concerns pressure difference. Do not add an atmospheric or other surface-pressure value unless an absolute-pressure model is explicitly introduced later.

figure.purpose: Resolve the area and path-length misconceptions
figure.brief: Make a two-part comparison. First show narrow and wide columns at equal depth with weight arrows proportional to area and matching area brackets. Second show two routes to the same lower level, one vertical and one sloping, with the same vertical delta-h bracket. Add no numerical answers.
figure.alt_text: Column area cancels and only vertical depth difference determines hydrostatic pressure difference.

blocks.title: The shortest reliable argument
content: For a column from a surface to a base, write V = Ah, m = ρV, W = mg and p = F/A. The shared area cancels.
For two points inside the liquid, balance an imaginary slab: lower pressure force equals upper pressure force plus the slab's weight. This gives Δp = ρgΔh directly.

Always state the assumptions: the fluid is static, density is uniform and Δh is a vertical depth difference. The next lesson will use the result more widely to solve for pressure difference, density or depth.
